Exporting to the EU? Three rules your EU buyers will ask you about before 30 December 2026

By Di Ban, Esq., Bandi & Associates PLLCPublished 2026-10-10Updated 2026-10-10

Published by Bandi & Associates PLLC · Tel. 925-375-2570 · 4322 Queens Street, Ste 1201, Long Island City, New York 11101

Also available in Chinese: 中文. The English page governs.

If you make or sell goods that end up in the European Union, three EU rules now reach you through your buyers and your listings rather than through any EU authority. The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) applies to large and medium operators from 30 December 2026: from that day your EU buyer cannot clear covered goods without a due diligence statement, and the data in it has to come from you. The green-claims rules in Directive (EU) 2024/825 have applied across the EU since 27 September 2026, with no transition period, to every listing and package sold to EU consumers. The Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) has applied since 12 August 2026 and requires a distance seller to appoint an authorised representative in each member state it sells into. This page explains who carries each obligation, what you will be asked for, and what you can prepare now. Dates were checked against the Official Journal on 10 October 2026; the EUDR date has been moved twice, so check again before you rely on it.

1. The three dates, and who the obligation falls on

Rule Date Who carries the legal obligation How it reaches you
EU Deforestation Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2025/2650 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/2102 Applies from 30 December 2026 to large and medium operators and traders; from 30 June 2027 to micro and small operators established by 31 December 2024, except for timber products already covered by the EU Timber Regulation, which stay on 30 December 2026 (Article 38) The "operator": the first person established in the EU who places the product on the EU market (Article 7). For a Chinese factory selling to an EU importer, that is the importer. Your buyer's supplier questionnaire and contract clauses. Without your data the buyer cannot file its statement.
Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition, Directive (EU) 2024/825 Member states apply it from 27 September 2026 (Article 4). No transition period. Any trader whose commercial communication reaches EU consumers, wherever the trader is. Marketplace take-downs, competitor warning letters in Germany, consumer-authority action in France.
Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2025/40 Applies from 12 August 2026; labelling rules from 12 August 2028 at the earliest; recyclability grades from 1 January 2030 at the earliest The "producer" of the packaging. A seller supplying end users in a member state where it has no establishment must appoint an authorised representative for extended producer responsibility in that member state (Article 45). Marketplace registration checks (Germany's LUCID register already), national registers, and your importer's questions when it sells under its own brand (Article 21).

A fourth rule is further out but uses the same evidence: the EU Forced Labour Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, applies from 14 December 2027 to all products and all operators, with no threshold. U.S. Customs has enforced the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act since June 2022 and had stopped more than 18,000 shipments for review by January 2026 (CBP's UFLPA statistics dashboard, which since 29 January 2026 counts by line rather than by shipment). A supply-chain map built for one serves the other.

2. EUDR: what your EU buyer will ask for

The EUDR covers seven commodities — cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood — and the products listed in its Annex I that contain or were made from them. For Chinese exporters the lists that matter most are wood (Harmonized System chapters 44, 47 and 48, and wooden seats, furniture and prefabricated buildings under 9401, 9403 and 9406) and rubber (the chapter 40 headings listed in Annex I, including tyres under 4011 and rubber gloves under 4015). A product is in scope only if its tariff line is listed in Annex I and it contains, has been fed with or has been made using one of the seven commodities (Article 2(2)). Regulation (EU) 2025/2650 removed printed books and other printed products (ex chapter 49) from Annex I from 26 December 2025. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/2102, in force since 18 September 2026, amended Annex I again; among other changes, rubber now means rubber of Hevea brasiliensis (synthetic-rubber goods such as nitrile gloves are outside), the wood lines do not cover bamboo or rattan, many wood and rubber lines exclude used and second-hand goods, conveyor belts (4010) and other vulcanised-rubber articles (4016) were removed, wooden seats under 9401 are now a list of subheadings, and cattle hides, skins and leather (ex 4101, ex 4104, ex 4107) were removed. From 30 December 2027 it also adds products, among them frozen cattle tongues (0206 21 00), coffee extracts and concentrates (2101 11 00) and a range of palm-oil derivatives, including certain soaps (3401) and polyethers (3907 29). Check both the line and the material.

Your buyer, as operator, must be able to show three things for every covered product (Article 3): that it is deforestation-free, that it was produced in accordance with the relevant legislation of the country of production, and that it is covered by a due diligence statement filed in the EU information system. To do that the buyer needs from you:

  • The geolocation of every plot of land where the commodity was produced. For a forest plot or a plantation this means coordinates; a plot over four hectares needs a polygon. The December 2025 amendment lets a micro or small "primary operator" (one established in a low-risk country that itself places on the market or exports what it grew or harvested) give the postal address of the plot or establishment instead (Article 4a(5)). It does not let a supplier replace coordinates in the data it gives an EU buyer: if your buyer is the operator, it still needs the geolocation.
  • The country of production, not the country of export. This is where many Chinese suppliers are exposed. China itself is classified as a low-risk country in the Commission's benchmarking (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1093), so a buyer sourcing Chinese-grown wood or rubber may use simplified due diligence. Russia, Belarus, Myanmar and North Korea are high-risk. Timber grown in Russia and processed in China keeps its Russian origin, and EU authorities have warned that Russian birch is relabelled in third countries, China among them. A furniture or plywood factory that cannot say where its logs grew cannot answer the questionnaire.
  • Evidence of legal production in the country of origin: harvesting permits, land-use rights, and the documents the buyer's own risk assessment names.
  • The reference number of any due diligence statement already filed upstream, if your supplier is itself an EU operator or trader.

Non-compliance is the buyer's problem in law: member states must provide for fines whose maximum is at least 4% of the operator's total annual EU-wide turnover, with confiscation of the goods and exclusion from public procurement (Article 25). In practice the buyer passes the problem to you through the contract — indemnities, audit rights, and the right to reject goods that arrive without the data. Read those clauses before you sign them.

One question Chinese suppliers raise is whether plot coordinates may be sent abroad at all. Industry reports describe suppliers refusing on security grounds. Published guidance from EU law firms takes the view that low-precision coordinates of agricultural or forest plots, shared for traceability, are unlikely to fall within the restrictions of China's surveying and mapping rules, but that is a question of Chinese law for a lawyer admitted in China. Before you send coordinates, decide with your own counsel what you will send, in what precision, and through which channel. We do not collect coordinates on this site and will not ask you to upload them.

3. Green claims: what has been banned since 27 September 2026

Directive (EU) 2024/825 added new items to the blacklist of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive — practices that are unfair in all circumstances, without any need to prove that a consumer was misled. Since 27 September 2026 these are prohibited in commercial communications to EU consumers:

  • A generic environmental claim — "eco-friendly", "green", "ecological", "sustainable", "climate friendly" and similar words in any language — unless the trader can demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim.
  • A sustainability label that is not based on a certification scheme or established by public authorities. A badge you designed yourself is such a label.
  • A claim that a product has a neutral, reduced or positive impact on the environment based on offsetting of greenhouse gas emissions — "carbon neutral", "climate neutral" and the like, where the neutrality is bought rather than achieved.
  • A claim about the whole product or the whole business when it concerns only one aspect — recycled packaging presented as a "sustainable product".

Where you will find these words: listing titles and bullet points, A+ content, packaging, the storefront page, product inserts and social-media posts. Images count as well as words. In Germany the rule is enforced largely by competitors and associations through formal warning letters that carry legal costs; in France the consumer authority has investigation and penalty powers and publishes its decisions. A listing that is live today can be the subject of a warning letter today.

The practical task is an inventory: every environmental statement, in every language, on every surface, with a decision against each — remove, keep with the evidence that supports it, or reword into a specific, verifiable statement ("the carton is made of 80% recycled fibre, certified by …"). The same inventory should be checked against U.S. rules — the Federal Trade Commission's Green Guides and, for goods sold in California, the state's limits on "recyclable" claims — because the same listing is usually live in both markets.

4. Packaging: the authorised-representative problem

PPWR replaced the 1994 packaging directive with a regulation that applies directly in all 27 member states from 12 August 2026. Its substantive design rules arrive in stages: harmonised labelling from 12 August 2028 at the earliest; recyclability performance grades, minimum recycled content and limits on empty space from 1 January 2030 at the earliest (each date moves later if the implementing acts come late). Two of its provisions reach non-EU sellers now:

  • Article 45. A producer that supplies packaged goods to end users in a member state where it is not established must appoint, by written mandate, an authorised representative for extended producer responsibility in that member state. There is no EU-wide representative: a seller shipping to German, French and Spanish consumers needs one in each. Germany has required registration in the LUCID register since 2019 and Amazon has blocked unregistered listings there since 2022; other member states are moving the same way.
  • Article 21. An importer or distributor that places packaging on the market under its own name or trademark is treated as the manufacturer and takes on the manufacturer's conformity obligations. If your EU customer sells your goods under its own brand, it will ask you for the packaging's technical data to meet that duty.

Appointing representatives, registering and paying fees is service-provider work, not legal work. We do not provide it, and we do not recommend providers for payment. Where this page or the Firm lists providers, the list is neutral, the ordering criteria are published, and any relationship is disclosed.

5. What the Firm does and does not do

Bandi & Associates PLLC is a New York law firm. Its responsible attorney, Di Ban, Esq., is admitted in New York and advises on U.S. federal and New York law: U.S. Customs enforcement under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, Lacey Act plant-product declarations (which since 1 December 2024 cover furniture and other wood products), Federal Trade Commission rules on environmental marketing, and the U.S.-law side of your contracts with buyers. Advice on EU law — the three regulations above and the member-state rules that implement them — is given by lawyers admitted in an EU member state with whom the Firm works as co-counsel; their identity, their role and the division of any fee are set out in writing before an engagement begins, and you may engage them separately if you prefer.

Two things the Firm does not do: it does not file due diligence statements or act as anyone's authorised representative in the EU, and it does not collect plot coordinates, employee data or identity documents through this site. If you ask the Firm to review a buyer questionnaire or a set of listings, the first step is a conflict check on the names of the parties, and nothing else is collected until that check is cleared and an engagement is signed.

6. What to prepare now

  1. List every product line you export to the EU with its tariff line, and mark which lines fall in EUDR Annex I.
  2. For each covered line, write down the country where the raw material grew and whether you can obtain plot data from your own supplier. Separate imported raw material from domestic.
  3. Pull every environmental word and image from your EU listings and packaging into one table, by market and language.
  4. For each member state you ship to directly, note whether you have an EPR authorised representative and a packaging registration number.
  5. If any input comes from a region U.S. Customs treats as high risk for forced labour, keep the purchase records, factory records and transport documents that trace it; the EU will ask for the same file from December 2027.
